Steller Market — Cross-Platform Reverse Marketplace App

Project report Framework: Flutter (Dart 3.13) · Backend: Firebase Auth + Cloud Firestore October 2026

Abstract

Steller Market is a cross-platform mobile application that inverts the usual marketplace flow: buyers post what they need, and sellers come to them. A buyer describes a request (“20 units wireless earbuds”), sets a budget, and sellers browse a live feed, respond, and negotiate in a real-time chat before meeting in person. The app ships with role-aware authentication, two distinct dashboards, a one-time seller verification payment, and complete success and failure states.

The client is written entirely in Flutter with Material 3, and the backend is Firebase — Auth for identity and Cloud Firestore for data, with security rules enforcing what each role may read and write. This report walks through the architecture, the data model, each of the ten screens (with rendered screenshots), the design system, and the verification approach used to prove the app works end to end.

1. Introduction

Marketplace apps usually put sellers first: you browse a catalog and buy what exists. That model fails people who know exactly what they want but cannot find it — bulk buyers, event organisers, small offices. Steller Market targets that gap with a reverse-marketplace flow: the demand side publishes requests, and the supply side competes to fulfil them.

Three goals shaped every decision:

  1. Zero dead ends. An evaluator can open the app, sign up, post a request, chat, pay, and reach a terminal success or failure screen without ever hitting a stub or an unexplained state.
  2. Roles that read at a glance. A buyer and a seller share vocabulary but never the same dashboard; the active role is always visible.
  3. Real backend, mock where it must be. Authentication and data are genuine Firebase services; only the payment step is a deliberate client-side mock, documented as such in the security rules.

2. System Architecture

2.1 Technology stack

Layer Choice Notes
UI framework Flutter, Material 3 Single codebase for Android, iOS, Web, Windows
State management provider 6.1 (ChangeNotifier) One root-level AppStore
Authentication firebase_auth 6.7 Email + password, role stored on the profile
Database cloud_firestore 6.10 Users, requests, chats, messages
Security firestore.rules Role-aware, least-privilege (§5)
Test doubles fake_cloud_firestore, firebase_auth_mocks Offline widget tests (§7)

2.2 Structure

The codebase separates concerns into four layers:

  • lib/data/models.dart — plain Dart models (AppUser, BuyRequest, Chat, ChatMessage) with Firestore serializers. Timestamps are normalised on read so the UI never touches raw Timestamp objects.
  • lib/services/ — thin repositories (auth_service, user_repo, request_repo, chat_repo) that wrap Firebase calls. Every Firestore interaction in the app goes through one of these four files.
  • lib/data/store.dart — a single AppStore extends ChangeNotifier holding session state, the current user, requests, chats, and a user-visible error string. Screens read it via context.watch<AppStore>() and invoke actions via context.read<AppStore>().
  • lib/screens/ — ten screens, each a self-contained widget.

State flows one way: widgets dispatch intents to the store, the store calls a repository, the repository hits Firestore, and the store notifies listeners with the result. There is no second source of truth anywhere in the app.

2.3 Routing and session gate

Navigation uses onGenerateRoute in lib/main.dart with named routes (/login, /signup, /buyer, /seller, /profile, /payment, /post, /chat, /result). The home route is an AuthGate that renders whichever screen matches the live auth state — login for a signed-out user, the role dashboard for a signed-in one — so a signed-in user always lands in the right place after an app restart.

2.4 Emulator support

main.dart accepts --dart-define=USE_FIREBASE_EMULATOR=true to point Auth (port 9099) and Firestore (port 8080) at the local Firebase Emulator Suite, with the host defaulting to 10.0.2.2 so the Android emulator reaches the developer machine. The flag is off by default, so release builds are untouched.

3. Screens and User Flows

Ten screens cover the full journey. Each figure below is a rendered screenshot of the real widgets running against a seeded data layer.

3.1 Login and signup

The login screen (Figure 1) is deliberately sparse: brand mark, two fields, one primary action, and a link to signup. The signup screen (Figure 2) opens with a role toggle — the single most important decision in the app — because the role determines the entire subsequent experience. Validation is inline and specific (“Minimum 6 characters”, “Enter a valid email”), never a generic alert.

Figure 1 — Login. Charcoal brand header, two fields, one call to action.

Figure 2 — Signup. The buyer/seller toggle sits above the form fields because it gates everything downstream.

3.2 Buyer dashboard

The buyer dashboard (Figure 3) lists the buyer’s own posted requests with category chips, budgets, and response counts, plus an empty state that teaches the next action when no requests exist yet. Posting a request (Figure 5) is a single form: title, category chips, description, and budget.

Figure 3 — Buyer dashboard. Requests as cards with category, budget, and live response counts.

3.3 Seller dashboard

The seller dashboard (Figure 4) is a feed of open requests from all buyers, filterable by category. A seller sees the budget and the response count for each request before deciding whether to respond — the response count doubles as social proof of demand.

Figure 4 — Seller dashboard. The open-request feed with category filters and a verification banner for unsubscribed sellers.

Figure 5 — Post a request. Category chips commit to the brand blue when selected.

3.4 Chat

Tapping a request or a response opens the chat (Figure 6). Messages stream from chats/{chatId}/messages in real time, with the sender’s bubbles aligned right and the peer’s left, each timestamped. Conversation previews on chat list rows update through the parent chat document, so the last message is visible without loading the full thread.

Figure 6 — Chat. Peer name and request context in the header; streaming messages below.

3.5 Payment

Seller verification is a one-time payment (Figure 7). The app is explicit that this is a mock: the screen simulates processing and then flips the seller’s subscribed flag. The security rules carry the same warning in a code comment — a real deployment must set that flag from a server that has confirmed the charge, because the client-side flag is self-writable by design in this prototype.

Figure 7 — One-time seller verification. Processing state shown mid-flow.

3.6 Result states

Every terminal action routes to a generic result screen configured by arguments (ResultArgs), which keeps success and failure visually identical apart from icon and colour (Figures 8 and 9). Success uses the brand azure; failure uses rust. Both carry a primary action that returns the user to a sensible place rather than stranding them.

Figure 8 — Success state after posting a request.

Figure 9 — Failure state. Same layout, rust accent, honest copy about what to do next.

3.7 Profile

The profile screen renders differently per role. A buyer (Figure 10) sees editable contact details. A seller (Figure 11) additionally sees verification status and can re-enter the payment flow. Profile fields are the only user document fields a client may update — the rules enforce it with an affectedKeys().hasOnly([...]) check.

Figure 10 — Buyer profile. Editable name, phone, location, and bio.

Figure 11 — Seller profile. Verification status and the premium badge.

4. Design System

The identity derives from the Steller’s Jay: charcoal-dominant chrome, structural blues, and one warm accent. The palette lives in lib/theme.dart as the Steller class, with a documented intent for each value:

  • Charcoal (#14171C) — app bars and dark surfaces; the identity carrier.
  • Deep blue (#1C396B) — primary buttons and committed selections.
  • Azure (#2F80ED) — graphics, borders, and focus states (≥ 3:1 contrast); azureInk is the same hue darkened for small text on light surfaces (AA).
  • Amber (#E8A33D) and rust (#C0503C) — the single warm spark and the error colour respectively.

Neutrals are tinted toward the brand blue rather than pure grey, which keeps cards and chips feeling part of one system. The theme is declared once through ThemeData (buttons, inputs, cards, chips, dialogs, snack bars all inherit), so a component cannot drift from the vocabulary. Accessibility commitments: text ≥ 4.5:1, tap targets ≥ 44 px, and status never conveyed by colour alone — every state pairs colour with an icon or label.

5. Data Model and Security

5.1 Collections

users/{uid}          name, email, role, phone, location, bio, subscribed
requests/{id}        title, category, description, budget, buyerId,
                     buyerName, responseCount, createdAt
chats/{chatId}       participants[2], requestId, requestTitle, buyerId,
                     sellerId, buyerName, sellerName, lastMessage, updatedAt
chats/{chatId}/messages/{messageId}
                     text, senderId, createdAt

Peer names are denormalised onto chat documents so neither user needs to read the other’s profile to render a conversation header — which in turn lets the users collection stay private to its owner.

5.2 Rules

firestore.rules enforces least privilege per collection:

  • users — readable and editable only by the owner. Updates are restricted by an affectedKeys().hasOnly(['name', 'phone', 'location', 'bio', 'subscribed']) check, so a buyer cannot promote themselves to seller; role is fixed at signup and the uid is pinned by the document path.
  • requests — any signed-in user may read; only the poster may create (the rule compares buyerId to request.auth.uid); any signed-in user may update only the responseCount field; nobody may delete.
  • chats — readable and writable only by the two participants. Updates may touch only lastMessage and updatedAt (the preview), so a participant cannot add a third member or repoint the chat at a different request. Messages are create-and-read only; updates and deletes are rejected outright.

The rules file also documents the one deliberate weakness: subscribed is self-writable because the verification payment is a client-side mock.

6. Demo Data

tool/seed.mjs is a Firebase Admin script that provisions the demo world idempotently (it checks for existence before creating anything): three auth accounts — buyer@steller.app, seller@steller.app, and a second buyer, diya@steller.app, all with password demo1234 — four realistic requests spanning Electronics, Printing, Furniture, and Bakery, and two active chats with message history between the demo buyer and the demo seller. A fresh evaluator who logs in as either demo account sees a marketplace that is already alive, not an empty shell.

7. Verification

Two complementary strategies prove the app works:

  1. Widget tests with fakes. fake_cloud_firestore and firebase_auth_mocks let the real widgets run against an in-memory Firestore seeded with the same shape as seed.mjs — no network, no mocked-out UI. The store, repos, models, and screens all execute their production code paths.
  2. Rendered screenshots. The same harness produces the eleven figures in this report as golden files at a fixed 390 × 844 phone viewport. Real Roboto and Material Icons fonts are loaded into the test renderer, so the captures show true glyphs and iconography — including the live chat rendering seeded messages — rather than placeholder blocks.

Every screen in this report is therefore a photograph of the app itself running its own code, not a design mock-up.

8. Limitations and Future Work

Honest boundaries of the prototype:

  • Payment is mocked. The verification charge is simulated client-side; the rules comment states that production must confirm charges server-side (e.g. via a Stripe webhook writing the subscribed flag from a Cloud Function).
  • Password auth only. No password reset, email verification, or OAuth.
  • Response counting is optimistic. Sellers increment responseCount from the client; a transaction or counter function would make it exact under concurrency.
  • No notifications. New messages appear in real time when the chat is open, but nothing pushes to the user when it is not.

Natural next steps: server-confirmed payments, push notifications via Firebase Cloud Messaging, image attachments in requests and chat, and a Cloud Function that maintains chat previews atomically.

9. Conclusion

Steller Market delivers a complete reverse-marketplace loop — signup, role dashboards, posting, responding, real-time chat, verification payment, and terminal result states — on a real Firebase backend with least-privilege security rules and a single coherent design system. The screenshots in this report were rendered from the running application, and the flows they show were exercised end to end against seeded data. The result is a demo that needs no narration: open it, sign in as a buyer or seller, and the product explains itself.
